page.title: Philosophical Keywords
page.subtitle: Core Epicurean concepts and imagery in the proem of Book III of De rerum natura

keywords.name: lumen
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 1, 22.

Metaphor of intellectual illumination central to Lucretius’ representation of Epicurus. The lumen symbolizes the clarity of scientific truth that dispels the darkness of superstition (tenebris tantis).
In line 22 (<foreign>large diffuso lumine ridet</foreign>), the radiant light evokes the serene condition of the gods, whose tranquility becomes a model for the Epicurean sage.
Across the poem, lumen functions as a recurring epistemological topos (cf. I 62; II 7), marking the transition from ignorance to rational understanding.

keywords.name: ratio
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 14, 44, 93.
The rational method and doctrinal system established by Epicurus, described as arising from a ‘divine mind’ (<foreign>divina mente coorta</foreign>).
In Book III, ratio introduces the investigation of the soul’s nature, grounding the argument against the fear of death.

At line 44 (<foreign>nostrae rationis</foreign>), Lucretius unmasks the boastful claims of those who pretend to have no need of natural philosophy, demonstrating that without rational inquiry true mental serenity remains unattainable.
At line 93 (naturae species ratioque) ratio closes the proem as the only force able to dispel the terrors and darkness of the mind, joined with the observation of nature (see naturae species).

keywords.name: moenia mundi
paragraphs: Occurrences: line 16.
The metaphorical ‘walls of the world’, representing the limits of traditional cosmological understanding.
Upon the revelation of Epicurean doctrine, these boundaries ‘fall apart’ (<foreign>discedunt</foreign>), allowing the philosopher to contemplate the infinite universe.
The image recalls heroic and military metaphors: Epicurus as a conqueror who breaks through the fortifications of ignorance.

keywords.name: inane
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 17, 27.
The void, one of the two fundamental principles of Epicurean physics alongside atoms (<foreign>corpora</foreign>).
Described as infinite, intangible, and without resistance, it enables all motion and atomic interaction (<foreign>totum video per inane geri res</foreign>).
Lucretius repeatedly emphasizes the necessity of the void to explain phenomena such as movement, growth, and natural change, confirming that the universe extends unbound beneath the observer's feet.

keywords.name: acherusia templa
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 25, 86.
The mythical realms and gloomy quarters of the underworld, named after the river Acheron (<foreign>Acherusia templa</foreign>).

Lucretius asserts that upon grasping the physical structure of the universe, these subterranean courts vanish entirely (<foreign>nusquam apparent</foreign>), since nature contains no punitive underworld for departed souls.

The archaic poetic phrasing underscores the traditional, mythological dread that Epicurean physics dismantles by demonstrating that nothing exists beneath the earth except boundless void and atomic motion.
At line 86 the phrase returns in a darker key: to escape the Acherusia templa (uitare Acherusia templa petentes), men betray their fatherland and their dear parents.

keywords.name: uoluptas
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 28, 40.
Pleasure understood as the supreme ethical good (<foreign>telos</foreign>) and the absence of mental and bodily pain in Epicurean doctrine.
At line 28, the sublime contemplation of cosmic laws generates a profound intellectual delight (<foreign>divina voluptas</foreign>) accompanied by reverent awe (<foreign>horror</foreign>).

Conversely, at line 40, the fear of death is exposed as a poison that contaminates human life from the bottom up, preventing any joy from remaining pure, clear, and unalloyed (<foreign>liquidam puramque</foreign>).

keywords.name: metus acheruntis
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 37, 64, 79.
The dread of death and post-mortem punishment personified by the underworld river Acheron (<foreign>metus ille... Acheruntis</foreign>).
Identified as the root cause of human anxiety and ethical degradation, it must be cast out headlong (<foreign>foras praeceps agendus</foreign>) through physical doctrine.
Lucretius reveals that this irrational terror undermines every aspect of mortal existence, driving individuals toward greed, political ambition, and moral crimes.
The same fear returns as <foreign>mortis formido</foreign> (lines 64, 79): it nourishes the wounds of life and can breed such hatred of life and light that men take their own lives (lines 79–82).

keywords.name: animus and anima
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 35, 36, 43, 54.

The dual components of the human soul in Epicurean psychology: the rational mind (<foreign>animus</foreign>), situated in the breast and responsible for thought and emotion, and the vital spirit (<foreign>anima</foreign>), dispersed throughout the whole body to transmit sensation.
Lucretius sets out to prove that both are corporeal compounds formed of extremely fine, smooth atoms, and consequently mortal and perishable.

Refuting rival beliefs that identify the mind with blood (<foreign>sanguis</foreign>) or wind (<foreign>ventus</foreign>), he demonstrates that both faculties dissolve completely when the bodily vessel breaks.

keywords.name: religio
paragraphs: Occurrences: line 54.
Superstitious terror and ritual obsession born from ignorance of natural causality, compelling mortals to propitiate imaginary gods and restless shades.

In lines 50–54, Lucretius shows that exiles and criminals who boast of philosophical self-sufficiency invariably relapse into superstitious rites (<foreign>parentant</foreign>, <foreign>inferias mittunt</foreign>) when adversity strikes.
The passage illustrates how adversity strips away hypocritical vanity, laying bare the deeply entrenched hold of <foreign>religio</foreign> on an unphilosophical mind.

keywords.name: tenebrae
paragraphs: Occurrences: lines 77, 88, 90, 91.

Darkness is the counter-image of the Epicurean lumen. At line 77 the envious complain that they wallow in darkness and mire (in tenebris uolui caenoque), excluded from the splendour of public honours.
In the simile of lines 87–90, children tremble at everything in the blind darkness (<foreign>caecis in tenebris</foreign>), just as adults fear empty phantoms in broad daylight.
At line 91 the image becomes wholly inward: the <foreign>tenebras animi</foreign> are dispelled not by the rays of the sun, but only by the observation of nature and reason.

keywords.name: pietas
paragraphs: Occurrences: line 84.
Dutiful devotion towards gods, family and fatherland, the cornerstone of traditional Roman morality.

Lucretius shows that the fear of death disturbs shame (pudor), breaks the bonds of friendship and overturns pietas from its foundations (in summa pietatem euertere fundo), so that men even betray their fatherland and parents (lines 85–86).
The passage reverses the traditional charge against Epicureanism: it is not philosophy but the fear of death that destroys piety.

keywords.name: naturae species
paragraphs: Occurrences: line 93.
The outward aspect and attentive observation of nature, which together with ratio forms the closing formula of the proem (naturae species ratioque).

The tercet of lines 91–93 repeats verbatim I 146–148 (and returns at II 59–61 and VI 39–41): only the understanding of nature, not the physical light of the sun, can dispel the terror and darkness of the mind (see tenebrae).
